title: Tomorrow, and commands
goal: Form the future in all four groups, give commands to one or many people, and forbid with noli.
bekal: tell the two future patterns apart and know which groups use which
make singular and plural commands from any verb

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Ante iter
dialogs.intro: The night before the trip. Quintus hands out jobs, and not all of them are welcomed.

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Cras ad villam ibimus. Mane surgetis!
lines.id: Tomorrow we're going to the farmhouse. You'll get up early!

notes: **Two patterns for one tense.** Groups I and II use *-bo, -bis, -bit* (*portabo*, *videbo*); groups III and IV use *-am, -es, -et* (*mittam*, *audiam*). There's no reason; these are leftovers of two different methods in the parent language, and both froze side by side in Latin.

**Mittet and mittit differ by one letter.** *Mittit* means "he sends", *mittet* means "he will send". A difference that small decides the meaning of the whole sentence, and it is one more reason why reading to the very last letter is non-negotiable.

**Porta! Audi! — commands are made by cutting.** Take the infinitive, cut off *-re*, and what is left is a command to one person: *portare* → *porta!*, *audire* → *audi!*, *videre* → *vide!*. For several people, add *-te*: *portate!*, *audite!*, *videte!* You have been using these since Unit 1 without noticing: *salve* and *salvete*, *vale* and *valete*.

**Noli, nolite — the polite "don't".** Latin does not forbid with *non* + command. It uses the command form of *nolo* ("be unwilling") plus the infinitive: *noli clamare!* — literally "be unwilling to shout". For several people: *nolite clamare!*

blocks.text: Which group uses which pattern is fixed once and for all, so as soon as you know a verb's group, you know its pattern.
Mixed group three follows group four: *facio* → *faciam, facies, faciet*. Note that only the "I" form of the second pattern ends in *-am*; the rest follow a tidy *-e-* pattern.

blocks.title: Traps you must recognize
items: *erunt* means "they will be"; *erant* means "they were". One letter moves the sentence from the future to the past.
*portabis* can never be confused with anything — the *-bo* pattern really is safer. It's the second pattern that needs your attention.

blocks.text: Commands have only two forms: one for one person, one for several. Both are made from the infinitive.

These four lose the final *e*, and only these four. Learn them as one string of sounds: *dic, duc, fac, fer*. You will meet them in famous sentences: *fac ut vivas* ("act so that you live") and *dic mihi* ("tell me").

blocks.title: Asking politely
items: *Quaeso* — "I beg you". Slipped into the middle of a sentence: *Dic mihi, quaeso.*
*Sis* (short for *si vis*, "if you want") — the equivalent of "please": *Veni, sis.*
*Amabo te* — literally "I will love you", used exactly like "pretty please": *Amabo te, tace!*
*Cave!* — "watch out!" This gives the sentence set into the floors of Roman houses: *Cave canem* — "beware of the dog".
To forbid, never use *non* + command. Always *noli* or *nolite* + infinitive.

blocks.text: Latin uses the future much more strictly than English. If the action hasn't happened yet, Latin demands the future — including in clauses where English uses the present ("if you come").

head: Latin
Translation
rows: Tomorrow we will go to the farmhouse.
I will wait for you in the morning.
You will see the sea and be able to swim.
If you come, I will be glad.

blocks.text: The fifth sentence uses a form not taught yet — *veneris*, "you will have come". Latin uses it in clauses whose action comes before the main one. You don't need to make it yourself; just recognize it when you meet it.

to go back, to return home
to head for, to ask for

exercises.prompt: Change to the future, keeping the same subject.
Fill in the blanks with the correct future form.
Make commands, first to one person, then to several.
